title: MNIST
body:
[[SGD Classification]]

---

70,000 handwritten digits, $28 \times 28$ greyscale, labelled 0 to 9. Modified National Institute
of Standards and Technology, hence the acronym. 60,000 training and 10,000 test, and the split is
part of the dataset rather than something you make.

It is the course's worked example and the standard first dataset everywhere, because it is small
enough to train on a laptop and hard enough to be worth doing. Flattened, each image is a 784-entry
[[Vector]], so a [[Neural Network]] on it has a 784-unit [[Input Layer]] and a 10-unit
[[Output Layer]] with a softmax.

The sequence the course runs:

1. **[[Binary Classification]] first**: "is this a 5", one output, [[Sigmoid]], [[Log Loss]].
2. **[[SGD Classification]]**: minibatch [[Gradient Descent]] rather than the full dataset.
3. **Ten classes**: softmax output, [[Cross-Entropy Loss]], a $10 \times 10$
   [[Confusion Matrix]] whose off-diagonal cells show which digits get confused (4 with 9, 3 with
   8).
4. **[[CNN]]**: the same problem with the spatial structure of the image respected instead of
   flattened away.

Two things it teaches beyond the mechanics. **Accuracy is nearly meaningful here** and almost
nowhere else, because the ten classes are roughly balanced, which makes it a good place to see why
the [[Confusion Matrix]] is needed once they are not. And step 4 is the clearest demonstration in
the course that architecture matters: flattening throws away the fact that adjacent pixels are
related, and a [[Multilayer Perceptron]] has to relearn that from data while a CNN gets it for
free.

Worth knowing that MNIST is now easy: convolutional models pass 99.5%, so a good score proves the
pipeline works rather than that the model is good.
